principle: Snap to a big lead-in pose on the frame the button is pressed
why: A smooth transition from standby into the windup takes too long. Jumping straight to a big pose tells players at once that their input was recognized, and it cues the opponent to dodge. Network and TV lag can never be fully eliminated, but the game can still acknowledge the input immediately; in Smash, responsiveness comes first.
how_to_apply: Skip easing frames out of standby: make the first frame after input a drastically different windup pose. For charge moves, hold that pose and shake in place while the button is held. Light, spammable moves can have no lead-in at all. If a windup reads as slow, have the character pull directly into the right pose rather than lengthening the ease.
anti_pattern: Interpolating from standby into the windup 'so the animation doesn't skip'; windups whose first frames barely change the silhouette.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the pose changes drastically on the press of a Smash Attack, then holds and shakes while charging. Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack comes out one frame after input; Final Fight's jab is instantaneous. Sora's Sonic Blade windup felt slow, so Sakurai had him pull directly into the right pose.
review_question: Does the very first frame after an attack press show a pose clearly different from standby?
keywords: lead-in anticipation windup wind-up startup first frame snap pose input acknowledgment responsiveness no easing charge attack

principle: Animate where and when the attack's collision actually is
why: A designer can make any animation connect by placing collision, but a large gap between visuals and collision feels wrong, and if the animation itself is mispositioned it feels even more broken. Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or that keep hitting after the swing, feel off. Because animation shapes game feel so much, animators can't leave gameplay to the designers.
how_to_apply: Give animators each attack's active frames and hitbox placement, and review attacks with collision displayed. Make the motion cross the median line where opponents stand and stay in the gameplay plane rather than angling toward or away from the camera. When a hit feels wrong, fix the arc or pose and the hitbox shape or timing together. Watch for stance changes on hit that move the target's top node.
anti_pattern: Animating without seeing collision; fixing a misplaced animation by stretching the hitbox; attacks angled toward the camera; a visible swing that outlasts its active frames without a reason.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: Pyra's forward aerial collision was shortened because it seemed to keep hitting after the swing; Mythra's slash was aligned to a diagonal; Steve's grab arc was pulled closer; Sacred Arrow's blade was raised slightly so it wouldn't pass straight through opponents; a neutral-attack combo missed because the target's top node moved back.
review_question: With collision displayed, does every attack's visible strike sit where and when its hitbox is active?
keywords: collision hitbox animation alignment active frames attack range median line gameplay plane hit detection animator responsibility top node root motion

principle: Make the hit stop frame the attack's strongest, clearest pose
why: Hit stop freezes the instant of contact, so that pose is the most memorable; everything hinges on it. On a finishing blow the screen stops completely, so a weak pose there is no good. In games about trading blows, attack animations affect fun more than any others.
how_to_apply: Treat the contact frame as a key pose: include it in reference photos and review it on its own. On sword swings, start collision partway into the swing once the pose is strong, and let hit stop kick in after the blade has swung out a bit. Check the pose on both the left and right of the screen.
anti_pattern: Collision on the first frame of motion, so hit stop freezes a half-formed pose; hit stop before the sword has swung out, which loses the 'hit' feeling.
example: Super Smash Bros.: sword-swing collision doesn't start until the sword is partway through; Pyra's hit pose before and after Sakurai's silhouette correction.
review_question: If you pause on the frame where each attack connects, is it the strongest, most readable pose in the move?
keywords: hit pose contact frame key pose hitstop pose impact frame attack pose freeze frame sword swing collision timing

principle: Exaggerate past "OK": too much is just right
why: Attacks are small things on a small screen, so the usual problem is 'not anywhere near far enough'; if a pose looks OK there's still room to push. Game characters lose much of the information real people give off and no part of them truly exists, so big performances make up for it. Pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness.
how_to_apply: Push twists, reach and extension past natural limits, until the rig's weighting nearly breaks. Treat motion capture as a starting point and make it bigger. Make a sword swing more than 'just a sword swing'. Scale exaggeration to the character's on-screen size and camera distance.
anti_pattern: Stopping at 'OK'; dropping motion capture straight into the game; keeping poses within what is physically possible.
example: Kazuya's Roundhouse to Triple Spin Kick twists so far it could look like a bug, and Sakurai says they should have gone further; Virtua Fighter's upper and lower body sometimes face opposite directions; Kinji Fukasaku's over-the-top Clock Tower 3 cutscenes.
review_question: For each key animation, did someone try a bigger version, and is the shipped one the biggest that still reads well?
keywords: exaggeration too much is just right push poses motion capture mocap cartoon big performances information loss rig limits

principle: Reach key poses fast; don't let interpolation water them down
why: Animation tools interpolate conveniently, but 'convenience doesn't mean quality': in-between frames overpower the key poses and make an animation feel slow even at the same length. Time saved on in-betweens goes to the lead-in and the strike, and key poses shown for even one frame each still leave an impression when the attack hits.
how_to_apply: Scrub interpolated attacks and cut in-between time so the key poses arrive quickly. Pull the windup further back, hold the anticipation relatively long, then pass through the key poses in as little as one frame each. Give poses more energy than the reference. Judge snappiness by eye in game, not by frame count.
anti_pattern: Accepting default interpolation between reference poses; judging speed only by frame count; mushy in-betweens on fast attacks.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: a kick recreated with straight interpolation felt too slow at 8 frames; the release version is still 8 frames and much snappier. Ryu's crouching heavy punch: forearm pulled back, anticipation held, the original's three key poses on screen one frame each.
review_question: Do your attacks hit their key poses quickly, or do in-between frames make them feel slow?
keywords: interpolation in-betweens key frames key poses snappy timing anticipation hold tweening easing curves slow animation

principle: Make the follow-through big, held and unlike standby
why: The hit is over in a fraction of a second; the follow-through takes the most screen time and shows what the character just did and how heavy it was. It is also the opening when the player can't act, so it must read clearly. The follow-through determines the impact of the attack itself.
how_to_apply: Keep the motion going with big movements that carry the strike's momentum before returning to standby. Hold a pose clearly different from standby. Give it its own trajectory instead of reversing the attack. Give landings a full follow-through, and place follow-throughs where they read from the game's camera.
anti_pattern: Interpolating straight back to idle; a follow-through that looks like standby; letting it fizzle out.
example: Ryu's uppercut follow-through in Smash Ultimate takes a different trajectory from the original's backwards playback; Sora's forward-aerial landing was reworked to follow through fully.
review_question: Does every recovery clearly show what move just happened and how heavy it was, right up to standby?
keywords: follow-through recovery animation end lag vulnerability weight momentum overlap settle return to idle

principle: Make the first damage frame an extreme pain pose
why: Hit stop holds the first frame of the damage animation, so it is what players actually see. A pose that looks nothing like standby makes it clear the character got hit even from far away, and both players feel the impact. 'The more punch, the better.'
how_to_apply: Author the hit-stop frame of each damage animation as an exaggerated, asymmetric pain pose, and segue into it with a quick blend from the pose at impact rather than a snap. Choose high, middle or low reactions by the nearest impact point and small, medium or large by strength, with a separate knockback set. Twist bodies in knockback so arms and legs read. Enter the damage animation immediately, even from special attacks.
anti_pattern: Damage poses close to standby; stiff bodies flying sideways; damage reactions that start late.
example: Super Smash Bros. damage reactions (nine ground types); Kirby's extreme damage pose in the Kirby Super Star design document; a fighter hit by a Final Smash should enter damage immediately; Wolf's damage face retouched for emphasis.
review_question: From the farthest gameplay camera, can you tell at a glance that a character just got hit, and how hard?
keywords: damage animation hit reaction flinch pain pose knockback pose hurt animation reaction set getting hit readability

principle: Pose for a clear, asymmetric silhouette from the game's camera
why: Smash is seen from the side, so profile silhouettes matter more than anything; one minor silhouette tweak can make a huge difference. Symmetric poses and plain sideways bends are dull, while a twist lets arms and legs read. A character's form should be exaggerated even in solid black, and if the basic pose is off nothing else saves it.
how_to_apply: Make all four limbs readable from the game's main view. Break symmetry unless it's deliberately comic. Twist the torso instead of bending it sideways; give torso, hips and legs different lines. Check poses on both sides of the screen and filled in solid black. Correct swing animations until the blade trail reads from the gameplay camera.
anti_pattern: Symmetric, front-facing poses; plain sideways bends; knockback bodies flying flat; horizontal slashes whose trails vanish from the side.
example: Pyra's pose before and after Sakurai's correction; Smash knockback poses twisted so limbs read; Sora's forward aerial, where upper-body twist brings more information to the pose; the Pit figma posed default and adjusted.
review_question: Filled in black and seen from the gameplay camera on both sides of the screen, is every key pose asymmetric and instantly readable?
keywords: silhouette pose posing asymmetry twist S-curve readability profile line of action dynamic pose solid black test

principle: Specify each animation's frames and key poses before animators start
why: Getting animation ideas across to the team is vital, and timings should be chosen with the game's push and pull in mind before animation begins. Four values are often enough for animators to start. A director needs a feel for frames to prepare this data and to catch errors when the build differs.
how_to_apply: Keep an animation list: every animation described in text with its length and when the attack occurs; mark loops like idle and walk 'Loop' or 'Any'. For each attack specify the standby pose, the attack pose, the attack start frame and the total frames until it can be canceled. Add photographed figure poses for key poses and source-game screenshots where relevant. Treat the spec as a first step; animators fill the gaps.
anti_pattern: Leaving timing to animators; describing timing in words; treating the director's spec as the finished animation.
example: Super Smash Bros. fighter spec sheets: an animation list plus photographed figure poses, 70 to 80 pages per fighter on average.
review_question: Does every animation request state its length, its attack start frame and its key poses?
keywords: animation list animation spec frame data timing sheet attack start frame total frames brief reference photos direction

principle: Judge animation in motion, at gameplay size and camera
why: A model can look warped when paused, and 'fixing' it kills the animation's energy. Motion that works up close feels far too understated when the character is small or far away. Faces in Smash are often too small to make out, and blade trails can nearly vanish from the side.
how_to_apply: Review attacks at full speed, at real in-game size and from the gameplay camera. Turn down corrections for distortions that only show in freeze-frames if the move reads in motion. For detailed checks use slow motion, hidden backgrounds and dev-mode transparency for capes and clothing.
anti_pattern: Approving animation in a close-up model viewer; correcting freeze-frame warps; judging faces at a size players never see.
example: Kazuya's twist looks like a bug when paused but reads well in motion; Smash Ultimate's developer mode can make capes translucent to check poses; slow-motion effect reference with backgrounds disabled.
review_question: Was this animation approved while playing at gameplay camera distance, or only in a paused close-up?
keywords: animation review in-game size camera distance freeze frame playback speed dev tools transparency slow motion review

principle: Keep blends short; use them for cancels, segues and directional poses
why: Blending lets the same follow-up animation start naturally from very different poses, but making animation too smooth reduces rhythm and impact, and automatic blends can distort the pose.
how_to_apply: When a cancel arrives, blend from the current pose into the new animation. Segue into damage poses with a quick blend (about four frames in Smash). Keep blend durations short and check them for distortion. Blend a fixed center stance with poses around a circle for directional moves. In full 3D, layer upper and lower body, place feet on terrain and let slopes affect turns.
anti_pattern: Long, smooth blends that sap rhythm; trusting automatic blends unchecked; snapping between unrelated poses on cancels.
example: Super Smash Bros.: idle-to-walk and attack-to-walk both look natural with the same walk; shield shifting blends circular movement with the center stance. Sakurai notes blending matters less in fast Smash than in fully 3D games.
review_question: Are your blends short enough to keep rhythm and free of distorted in-between poses?
keywords: animation blending crossfade transition cancel blend blend duration layered animation foot placement directional blend

principle: Squash and stretch while keeping volume constant
why: Rotation and translation are everywhere, but scaling is often overlooked; with it a bouncing ball feels almost touchable, and squash and stretch gives objects texture and life. Keeping mass roughly constant is what sells it: 3D Kirby squashed only vertically lost his physical presence.
how_to_apply: Add squash to landings, crouches and bounces and compare with and without. When squashing on one axis, widen the others. On 3D models, sculpt the squashed shape (an oval-track profile, a blend shape) instead of scaling one axis. Use shape animation for cartoon squeezes a skeleton can't do.
anti_pattern: Squashing vertically without widening ('your oval will end up dull'); treating rotation and translation as the whole toolkit.
example: Kirby has squashed on crouches and landings since the Game Boy; Sakurai's Daily Report asked for side volume on the 3D model; Tom and Jerry-style squeezing might need shape animation in CG.
review_question: Where landings, crouches and impacts squash, does the volume stay about the same?
keywords: squash and stretch scaling volume preservation mass bounce landing crouch blend shapes shape animation

principle: Move bodies like bodies: two axes, linked joints, bent wrists
why: A head turned on one axis looks mechanical and a one-axis wrist twist looks like a drill. Connected parts move together in reality. Wrists that follow a straight line from the arm look limp, and a perpendicular grip on a swung object makes a character look like an action figure.
how_to_apply: Layer a dip (X) or tilt (Z) onto every Y-axis turn of heads, wrists and torsos. Move the shoulder and collarbone with a twisting wrist. Bend wrists rather than keeping them in line with the arm. Pose anything swung with the forearm in a diagonal grip. Plan head turns with the eye line, and reduce the head turn once the eyes carry part of the look.
anti_pattern: Single-axis organic rotation; straight wrists; perpendicular grips on swords and bats; full head turns animated before the eyes exist.
example: Sakurai's own head turn; revving a motorcycle (shoulder and collarbone move with the wrist); Sora's losing clap, limp until the wrists bent; diagonal versus perpendicular weapon grips.
review_question: Does any organic motion rotate on a single axis or move a joint without the joints connected to it?
keywords: two-axis rotation head turn wrist twist joints collarbone shoulder grip fingers diagonal grip organic motion eye line

principle: Give mechanical motion personality: off-center pivots, wobble and recoil
why: Designers tend to move things in straight lines and smooth circles, but animation means putting a soul into something unmoving, and software defaults look bland. A slightly shifted rotation axis feels a little erratic and organic, a wobble makes a straight shot fun to watch, and recoil makes firing feel forceful.
how_to_apply: Move the pivot of thrown or spinning objects and swung weapons slightly off the geometric center or grip. Layer a small looping offset onto straight-flying projectiles. Snap guns or cannons back on each shot. Hand-tune rotation timing (offset the two axes, add an occasional counter-motion) instead of trusting generated curves. Make quick mock-ups during review to show the alternative.
anti_pattern: Straight-line moves and center-point rotations left as the software produced them.
example: Kirby's Shotzo 'wobbly cannonballs' (a six-frame offset loop); Smash Ultimate's bomb throw spins on an off-center axis; Pyra's Blazing End axis was moved off the sword's grip; Star Force's side cannons pull back with each missile.
review_question: Which moving objects still follow straight lines or spin on their exact center, and what would give each one personality?
keywords: pivot center of rotation off-center axis wobble projectile motion recoil function curves software defaults personality secondary motion

principle: Build rigs that allow exaggeration from the start
why: Rigs that lock arms to the torso make adequate animation impossible. Joints are naturally limited to 180 degrees, but bending past straight adds oomph; backward-bending joints make IK flip, and fixes like extra joints cost processing and need cartoon-minded animators. Convenient tools also set mental limits.
how_to_apply: Decide early whether the style needs exaggeration. Rig shoulders to move forward and back and the upper and lower body to rotate independently. Budget extra joints or an extended skeleton for limbs that bend past straight, watch for IK flipping, and hire or brief animators with cartoon sensibilities. Where processing is tight, lock finger joints and swap preset finger patterns.
anti_pattern: Letting a standard rig decide what poses are possible; adding exaggeration needs late, when the rig can't support it.
example: The first Smash (or Dragon King prototype) had arms rigged directly to the torso; Sakurai proposed past-straight joints at the start of Smash development, but processing load and staffing left it unsolved.
review_question: Can your rig hit the most exaggerated pose your style calls for, and was that decided before animation began?
keywords: rig rigging skeleton joints IK FK range of motion exaggeration extra joints processing load fingers

principle: Keep faces toward the viewer in side-view games
why: Without mirroring, the character on the right faces away, so you can't see their expression and get little information. Pure profile views aren't fun to look at and hide the face for half the movement. Non-realistic tricks like moving the mouth to the side of a profile face can express a character better than anatomy.
how_to_apply: Mirror the animation set when a character changes facing instead of turning the model around. Angle runs and similar moves diagonally toward the camera. Plan for flipped handedness and quick item hand-swaps; skip mirroring for asymmetric characters such as sword fighters. Make emblems and lettering mirror-safe. Try placing the mouth on the side of the face in profile.
anti_pattern: Expressive characters showing the back of their head on one side; runs in pure profile; rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic.
example: Smash Bros. adopted flipped animation after Brawl; Kirby's run angles toward the camera; Street Fighter II mirrored sprites and IV kept it; Mega Man Legends and Sonic put the mouth on the side of the face.
review_question: Can players see the face of every expressive character from both sides of the screen?
keywords: flipped animation mirroring facing side view face visibility handedness profile mouth manga conventions

principle: Push facial expressions a step past done, shaped by anatomy
why: CG loses information, so 'too much is about right' for realistic and cartoony faces alike; most artwork Sakurai received had expression shifts that were too small. Details tied to anatomy sell an expression. Where the source has no facial range, putting the source first matters more than adding faces.
how_to_apply: Once an expression feels done, make it one step bigger and judge it at in-game size. Show eye white above and below the iris on wide eyes, offset upper and lower teeth, and size mouth shapes to the jaw. Retouch key expressions before modeling. If the character only blinks in the source, carry emotion through body movement.
anti_pattern: Subtle expressions on small on-screen faces; inventing faces the source character lacks.
example: Smash Ultimate: Wolf's damage face retouched to suit a wolf's jaw; Kazuya's brows pulled up to look angrier; Steve only blinks, so his movement does the work; a Sora costume's damage expression was too weak.
review_question: At the size players see them, do faces read clearly, and do they stay true to the source?
keywords: facial animation expressions faces exaggeration eye whites teeth jaw retouch expression strength

principle: Give movement weight, and give fast motions enough frames to register
why: Motions that are too fast don't land: Kazuya's wings retracting in two frames had no impact. Normal legs can't keep up with very fast movement. Weight shifts and solid landings make movement believable, and slipping feet read as wrong.
how_to_apply: Add frames to secondary motions that vanish before they register. For speeds a walk cycle can't support, use bounding or sliding locomotion. Shift weight forward in walks to improve weight and silhouette. Keep feet planted on landing. Add squash on landings.
anti_pattern: Sped-up realistic leg cycles; secondary motion too quick to see; sliding feet.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Pit bounds and slides because normal legs couldn't keep up; Kazuya's wing retraction got more frames; Pyra's walk shifts her weight forward; Sora's landing foot moved too far.
review_question: Is any motion so fast it never registers, or so smooth it has no weight?
keywords: locomotion walk run cycle weight landing foot sliding secondary motion frames wings bounding

principle: Honor the source's feeling, not its literal frames
why: 2D poses don't survive a literal move to 3D, and copying a source exactly can miss what makes it feel right. Sakurai's rule is to honor the feeling and do what works best, keeping signature poses and limits where the source has them.
how_to_apply: Keep a source character's signature poses and quirks, but change what the new medium needs: a different first frame for momentum, a new follow-through path instead of reverse playback. Put source screenshots next to your version and compare feel, not just shapes. Keep source limitations (a face that only blinks) and compensate elsewhere.
anti_pattern: Playing source poses forward then backward in 3D; matching a reference exactly but missing the character.
example: Ryu's uppercut in Smash Ultimate; Kazuya's spin kick twist and knocked-down pose kept from his original game; Steve's blink-only face; the Nakoruru Mii costume revised until it felt like her.
review_question: Does each adapted move feel like its source in play, even where the frames differ?
keywords: source material faithfulness adaptation 2D to 3D guest characters licensed characters signature moves honor the original

principle: Check every variant: ground and air, every direction, both facings
why: Variants drift apart: Sora's Sonic Blade had drastically different ground and aerial poses and lost reach when aimed upward, which counts as a bug. Poses look different on the left of the screen than the right, and a stance change on hit can push a target out of a combo.
how_to_apply: Play ground and aerial versions of every special side by side, comparing poses and reach. Test attacks aimed in each direction. Review poses on both screen sides. Run multi-hit strings against every reaction stance.
anti_pattern: Reviewing only the default version of a move; assuming mirrored or aerial variants inherit correctness.
example: Smash Ultimate: Sora's Sonic Blade fixed for pose mismatch and upward reach; a neutral-attack combo that missed because of a stance change.
review_question: Has every move been checked in its ground, aerial, directional and mirrored versions?
keywords: animation QA variants ground aerial versions directions mirrored poses stance combos consistency

principle: Find and communicate poses with a physical figure
why: Handling a physical figure teaches what makes a pose cool and which angle works best; there's no formula for posing. A posed, photographed figure communicates key poses to animators more clearly than words, and showing beats telling in feedback.
how_to_apply: Keep a posable figure at your desk and practice posing it, including zooming it around ('bundodo'). For specs, pose it, photograph it, cut out the silhouette and raise the contrast. In reviews, show a posed figure or a retouched frame rather than describing the change.
anti_pattern: Describing poses only in text; polishing details while the base pose is off.
example: Sakurai's Pit figma; Smash spec sheets with photographed figure poses; Sora's forward aerial explained with a posed figure.
review_question: When you ask for a pose change, do you show the pose instead of describing it?
keywords: posing action figure figma reference photos bundodo pose reference feedback visual direction
